blocks.content: A request that has been routed to the right handler and deserialized into a clean object is still, in a real sense, a stranger. It arrived from outside your system, and outside your system is exactly where you have the least control. The client could be a well behaved app, a browser extension, a curl command someone typed by hand, or a script deliberately trying to break something. Nothing about deserialization tells you which.

So before that object is allowed anywhere near your business logic, one more question has to be answered: is this data actually what it claims to be. Checking that is validation. Reshaping the data into exactly the form the rest of the system expects, once it has passed those checks, is transformation. Together they form the last gate a request passes through before it is trusted.

It helps to think of this stage as airport security rather than a polite front desk. A front desk assumes you belong there. Security assumes nothing, checks everyone the same way regardless of how confident they look, and only lets through what has actually been verified. That is the posture this topic is about.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396530479-66195994.png
blocks.alt: Validation treats every incoming request like airport security does, checking it the same way regardless of how trustworthy it looks

blocks.content: 1. Why Validation Has to Happen at the Boundary
blocks.text: 1. Why Validation Has to Happen at the Boundary

blocks.content: The single rule underneath everything in this topic is short enough to memorise: never trust client input. Not because clients are usually malicious, most are not, but because your server has no way to distinguish a malicious request from a merely buggy one just by looking at where it came from. A mobile app with an old cached form, a partner integration with a typo in their code, and an actual attacker probing your API all produce the exact same thing from your server point of view: a request whose contents you did not create and cannot vouch for.

blocks.title: The one line version
blocks.content: Validation is the practice of checking that incoming data is correct, complete, and safe before any code that assumes it is correct gets to run.

The word boundary matters as much as the word validation. This checking has to happen at the edge of your system, on every request, before the data goes anywhere. A validation check buried deep inside a function that only sometimes gets called is not a boundary check, it is a hope. The boundary is where trust changes from none to some, and that transition should happen in one deliberate, consistent place.

This is also why validation cannot be skipped just because a client side form already checked the same fields. Client side validation is a courtesy for honest users with slow connections, giving them fast feedback without a round trip. It is not a security control, because any client side check can be bypassed entirely by calling the API directly. The server side check is the one that actually protects the system.

blocks.title: What skipping the boundary check looks like
blocks.text: A checkout form limits quantity to 10 in the browser using a dropdown. Nothing stops a request sent directly to the API from setting quantity to negative one thousand. Without a server side check, that request reaches inventory logic exactly as written, and inventory logic was never built to handle a negative quantity.

blocks.title: The client is a suggestion, not a guarantee
blocks.content: Anything shipped to a browser or a mobile app, including its validation logic, can be inspected, modified, or ignored entirely by whoever controls the device it runs on.
2. Validation vs Sanitization vs Transformation
blocks.text: 2. Validation vs Sanitization vs Transformation

blocks.content: These three words get used almost interchangeably in casual conversation, but they describe genuinely different operations, and mixing them up leads to sloppy code.

{"headers":["Operation","What It Does","Example"],"rows":[["Validation","Checks data against rules and accepts or rejects it","Reject a request where email is missing"],["Sanitization","Removes or neutralizes dangerous content from data","Strip HTML tags from a comment before storing it"],["Transformation","Reshapes data into the type or format the system expects","Convert the string \"42\" into the number 42"]]}

Validation is a yes or no question: does this data satisfy the rules, and if not, the request is rejected outright. Sanitization changes the data itself to remove something unsafe, letting the request continue with a cleaned up version rather than rejecting it. Transformation changes the data shape or type without any judgment about safety at all, purely to make it usable by the rest of the system.

blocks.title: They usually happen together, not instead of each other
blocks.content: A single incoming field often passes through more than one of these in sequence: trimmed and normalized, then validated against a rule, then transformed into its final type. Treating them as one blurry step is where bugs creep in.

blocks.title: One field, all three operations
blocks.text: A comment field arrives as " Great post! ". Sanitization strips the HTML tags. Validation confirms the remaining text is under the maximum length. Transformation trims the leading and trailing whitespace, leaving a clean "Great post!" ready to store.

blocks.content: 3. Where This Fits in the Pipeline
blocks.text: 3. Where This Fits in the Pipeline

blocks.content: This topic closes out a three part journey through the earliest moments of a request. Routing matched the method and path to a handler. Serialization and Deserialization turned the raw request body into a usable, typed object. Validation and transformation is the final check before that object is allowed to reach actual business logic.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785276126160-867710827.png
blocks.alt: Validation and transformation run after deserialization and before business logic, since raw bytes cannot be validated directly

blocks.content: The ordering here is not a stylistic choice, it is a dependency. You cannot validate a field type or a business rule against raw, undeserialized bytes, so validation has to run after deserialization has already produced a structured object. And it has to run before any database write, external call, or state change, because once a side effect has happened, rejecting the request afterward cannot undo it.

blocks.title: A useful mental checkpoint
blocks.content: By the time your business logic function is called, everything it receives should already be routed, deserialized, validated, and transformed. If a handler still needs to defensively check whether a field exists, validation upstream has a gap.
4. Schema Based Validation
blocks.text: 4. Schema Based Validation

blocks.content: Writing validation rules by hand, one if statement per field, works for a handful of fields and becomes unmanageable fast. Most real systems instead declare a schema, a structured description of what a valid request looks like, and hand that schema to a validation library that checks incoming data against it in one pass.
JSON Schema style validation
blocks.text: JSON Schema style validation

blocks.content: JSON Schema describes the shape of a JSON document declaratively: which fields are required, what type each one must be, and constraints like minimum values or string patterns. A validator reads the schema and the incoming payload together and reports every place they disagree.
DTO based validation
blocks.text: DTO based validation

blocks.content: Typed languages often take a different route: define a class, called a Data Transfer Object or DTO, with validation rules attached directly to its fields as annotations or decorators. The framework validates an incoming payload against that class automatically before the handler method even runs.

Both approaches solve the same problem from opposite directions. JSON Schema describes validation as data, which is language agnostic and easy to share across services. DTO based validation describes it as code, which integrates tightly with a typed language and gives you compiler support, at the cost of being tied to one language and framework.
Fluent, programmatic validators
blocks.text: Fluent, programmatic validators

blocks.content: A third style, common in JavaScript and TypeScript backends through libraries like Zod or Joi, builds a schema by chaining function calls rather than writing a static declaration. It sits somewhere between the two earlier styles: still declarative in spirit, but expressed directly in code, which makes it easy to reuse, compose, and even infer a static type from automatically.

Whichever style a team picks, the underlying goal is identical: describe what valid input looks like once, in one place, and let a library enforce it consistently rather than trusting every handler to remember every rule.
5. Validating Types vs Business Rules
blocks.text: 5. Validating Types vs Business Rules

blocks.content: Not all validation checks are the same kind of check, and it helps to separate them explicitly. A type check asks a narrow, mechanical question: is this field the kind of value it claims to be, a string, a number, a boolean, a valid date. A business rule check asks a domain specific question that only makes sense with knowledge of what the system is actually for: is this discount percentage under the maximum allowed, is this username already taken, is this booking date in the future.

["Type checks are generic and reusable across any project: is it a string, is it a number, is it a valid email format.","Business rule checks are specific to your domain: is the requested quantity in stock, is the user allowed to perform this action, does this date range make sense.","Type checks can usually run entirely from the schema alone, with no database access needed.","Business rule checks often need to consult application state, such as checking a database for uniqueness or availability."]
items: Type checks are generic and reusable across any project: is it a string, is it a number, is it a valid email format.
Business rule checks are specific to your domain: is the requested quantity in stock, is the user allowed to perform this action, does this date range make sense.
Type checks can usually run entirely from the schema alone, with no database access needed.
Business rule checks often need to consult application state, such as checking a database for uniqueness or availability.

blocks.content: Schema based validation, described in the previous section, is naturally suited to type checks, since a schema is a static description that does not know anything about your database. Business rules typically need a further, explicit validation step written as application code, run after the schema check has already passed, precisely because they need information the schema alone cannot express.

{"headers":["Check","Question Asked","Needs Application State"],"rows":[["Type check","Is age a number","No"],["Format check","Is email shaped like an email address","No"],["Business rule","Is this email already registered","Yes, a database lookup"],["Business rule","Is the requested seat still available","Yes, current inventory"]]}
A schema can tell you a field is a well formed email address. Only your application can tell you whether that email already belongs to someone else.
6. Transformation: Reshaping Data Into What the System Expects
blocks.text: 6. Transformation: Reshaping Data Into What the System Expects

blocks.content: Even after data has passed every validation check, it is not always in the shape your code actually wants to work with. Transformation is the step that closes that remaining gap, converting technically valid input into the exact types and structures the rest of the system assumes it will receive.

["String to boolean: the query parameter \"true\" becomes the boolean value true, not the truthy string \"true\".","String to date: an ISO date string like \"2026-07-21\" becomes an actual Date object your code can compare and format.","Trimming and normalizing: leading and trailing whitespace removed, email addresses lowercased for consistent comparison.","Default values: an optional field that was omitted gets filled in with a sensible default rather than staying undefined.","Coercing numeric strings: a query parameter like page=2, which always arrives as a string, becomes the number 2."]
items: String to boolean: the query parameter "true" becomes the boolean value true, not the truthy string "true".
String to date: an ISO date string like "2026-07-21" becomes an actual Date object your code can compare and format.
Trimming and normalizing: leading and trailing whitespace removed, email addresses lowercased for consistent comparison.
Default values: an optional field that was omitted gets filled in with a sensible default rather than staying undefined.
Coercing numeric strings: a query parameter like page=2, which always arrives as a string, becomes the number 2.

blocks.title: A concrete transformation
blocks.text: A client sends { "subscribed": "true", "signupDate": "2026-07-21" }. After transformation, the handler receives { subscribed: true, signupDate: Date(2026-07-21) }, values it can use directly in conditionals and date arithmetic without any further parsing.

blocks.title: Transform after validating, not before
blocks.content: Validating the raw string "true" as a boolean-shaped value, then transforming it into an actual boolean, keeps the two concerns separate. Transforming first and validating the result can hide the fact that the original input was malformed.
7. Fail Fast vs Collect All Errors
blocks.text: 7. Fail Fast vs Collect All Errors

blocks.content: When a request fails validation on more than one field at once, there are two reasonable ways to respond, and they produce noticeably different developer experiences. Fail fast stops at the very first invalid field and returns immediately. Collect all errors checks every field regardless of earlier failures and returns the complete list at once.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785276127813-538124638.png
blocks.alt: Fail fast stops at the first invalid field, collecting all errors reports every failure in one response

blocks.content: {"headers":["Strategy","Behavior","Best For"],"rows":[["Fail fast","Stops and returns on the first invalid field","Simple internal APIs, performance sensitive checks"],["Collect all errors","Checks every field and returns the full list","Public facing forms and APIs with many fields"]]}

Fail fast is simpler to implement and slightly cheaper to run, since it can stop as soon as it finds a problem. Collect all errors is friendlier to the caller, especially for a form with a dozen fields, since a client can fix every problem in one round trip instead of discovering them one at a time through repeated submissions.

blocks.title: Most public APIs pick collect all
blocks.content: A frustrating experience is submitting a form, fixing the one error shown, resubmitting, and getting told about a second unrelated error that was true all along. Public facing validation almost always collects everything it can before responding.
8. Security Implications of Skipping Validation
blocks.text: 8. Security Implications of Skipping Validation

blocks.content: Validation is not only about good data hygiene, it is a genuine security control. A large share of classic web vulnerabilities exist specifically because untrusted input reached sensitive code without being checked first.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396530480-316188821.png
blocks.alt: Untrusted input that skips validation and reaches a query or page render directly opens the door to SQL injection or XSS

blocks.content: SQL injection happens when untrusted input is concatenated directly into a database query, letting an attacker supply text that changes the query structure itself rather than just its data. Cross site scripting happens when untrusted input is rendered into a page without being escaped, letting an attacker run their own script in another user browser. Both are, at their core, a failure to validate or sanitize input before it reached a context where it could do damage.

The same underlying pattern repeats across other injection families that are worth naming, since interviewers and security reviews both look for awareness of the full category, not just SQL injection alone.

{"headers":["Attack","Unsafe Sink","Validation Defense"],"rows":[["SQL injection","A database query built with string concatenation","Use parameterized queries and reject unexpected characters"],["Cross site scripting","HTML rendered without escaping","Sanitize or escape output, validate input length and content"],["Command injection","A shell command built from user input","Avoid shelling out at all, or strictly allow list arguments"],["NoSQL injection","A query object built from raw request fields","Reject unexpected operators like $where in input objects"]]}

blocks.title: Validation is a security layer, not a courtesy
blocks.content: Rejecting malformed or unexpected input before it reaches a query, a template, or a shell command closes off entire categories of injection attacks before they can even be attempted.
Every field you do not validate is a field an attacker gets to define the rules for instead of you.
9. Validation Layers: Client, Gateway, and Service
blocks.text: 9. Validation Layers: Client, Gateway, and Service

blocks.content: Validation often happens in more than one place in a real system, and it helps to be clear about what each layer is actually for. Client side validation, in a browser form or a mobile app, exists purely for user experience, giving instant feedback without a network round trip. An API gateway may perform lightweight validation too, rejecting obviously malformed requests before they even reach a backend service, mostly to reduce wasted load.

The service itself, the one described throughout this topic, performs the authoritative validation. It is the only layer that cannot be bypassed, because every legitimate path to changing data eventually flows through it. Client and gateway checks are optimizations that reduce unnecessary traffic. Service level validation is the actual security and correctness boundary.

blocks.title: Defense in depth, not defense in one place
blocks.content: Multiple validation layers are not redundant, they serve different goals: speed for the client, load reduction for the gateway, and correctness guarantees for the service. Removing the service level check because a gateway already checks something is a common and serious mistake.
10. Schema Based Validation in Practice: A DTO Walkthrough
blocks.text: 10. Schema Based Validation in Practice: A DTO Walkthrough

blocks.content: Putting the earlier sections together, a typical request flows through a predictable sequence once it reaches the service layer: the raw, deserialized object is checked against a schema or DTO, type mismatches and missing required fields are rejected immediately, and only a request that passes is handed off, transformed, to the actual handler function.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785276130951-416815760.png
blocks.alt: A DTO schema check either rejects a request outright or guarantees the handler receives an object in exactly the expected shape

blocks.content: Notice that the handler function itself contains no defensive checks at all. It simply trusts that anything reaching it has already been validated, because the middleware in front of it made that guarantee. This is the entire point of doing validation at a consistent boundary: business logic gets to stay focused on business logic.

The same shape shows up in a Java Spring service, just expressed through annotations instead of middleware. The @Valid annotation tells the framework to validate the incoming body against the DTO before the method body ever executes.
11. Common Pitfalls
blocks.text: 11. Common Pitfalls

blocks.content: A handful of mistakes account for most of the real world bugs and incidents tied to validation.

["Trusting client side validation as if it were a security control, when it can be bypassed by calling the API directly.","Validating types but skipping business rules, letting through requests that are structurally fine but logically nonsensical.","Inconsistent validation across endpoints, where one route checks a field strictly and another accepts almost anything.","Returning overly detailed error messages that reveal internal implementation details an attacker could use.","Mutating input during validation instead of during a clearly separate transformation step, making bugs hard to trace."]
items: Trusting client side validation as if it were a security control, when it can be bypassed by calling the API directly.
Validating types but skipping business rules, letting through requests that are structurally fine but logically nonsensical.
Inconsistent validation across endpoints, where one route checks a field strictly and another accepts almost anything.
Returning overly detailed error messages that reveal internal implementation details an attacker could use.
Mutating input during validation instead of during a clearly separate transformation step, making bugs hard to trace.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Pitfall","Typical Fix"],"rows":[["Relying on client side checks alone","Always re-validate on the server, treating the client as untrusted"],["Skipping business rule checks","Add an explicit rule check after the schema check passes"],["Inconsistent rules across endpoints","Share one validation schema or DTO across every route touching the same resource"],["Leaky error messages","Return generic, field level errors without internal stack traces or query text"]]}

blocks.title: A cheap habit that catches most of these
blocks.content: Write one test per field that sends an obviously invalid value and asserts the request is rejected with a 4xx status. Running this across every endpoint quickly surfaces routes that forgot validation entirely.
12. How to Talk About This in an Interview
blocks.text: 12. How to Talk About This in an Interview

blocks.content: When an interview question involves designing an API endpoint, mentioning validation explicitly, and being precise about where it sits, is one of the fastest ways to show maturity beyond just drawing boxes and arrows on a whiteboard.
State the boundary: I explain that I validate every request at the service boundary, immediately after deserialization, regardless of whether a gateway or client already checked something.
Name the schema: I describe using a schema or DTO shared consistently across a resource, so every endpoint touching it enforces the same rules instead of quietly drifting apart over time.

Separate types from business rules: I call out that structural checks come from the schema, while domain specific rules, like uniqueness or availability, need an explicit extra step against application state.
Mention the security angle: I connect validation directly to preventing injection style attacks, showing I understand it as a security control, not just a data hygiene step.
Close the loop: I tie it back to the earlier stages, routing selects the handler, deserialization produces an object, and validation is what finally makes that object safe to act on.
13. Common Questions
blocks.text: 13. Common Questions

blocks.content: Is client side validation ever useful? Yes, for user experience. It gives instant feedback without a network round trip, but it must never be treated as a substitute for server side validation, since it can always be bypassed.

Where exactly does validation run relative to deserialization? Always after. Deserialization turns raw bytes into a structured object first; validation then checks that object, because you cannot apply type or business rules to bytes that have not been parsed yet.

Should I fail fast or collect all errors? For public facing APIs and forms, collect all errors so users can fix everything in one pass. For simple internal checks where performance matters more than experience, fail fast is often good enough.

What is the difference between sanitization and validation? Validation accepts or rejects data based on rules. Sanitization modifies data to remove something unsafe while still allowing the request through. They solve different problems and are often used together.

Why does skipping validation lead to injection attacks? Because unvalidated input can carry content, such as SQL syntax or script tags, that changes the meaning of a query or a page instead of just supplying data for it. Rejecting or properly escaping unexpected input closes that door.

Can validation and transformation share one library? Often, yes. Many modern validation libraries validate and transform in the same call, returning either a list of errors or a fully typed, transformed object, which is convenient as long as the two concerns stay conceptually distinct in how you reason about them.

Does every field need a business rule check? No. Most fields only need type and format validation. Business rule checks are reserved for fields where domain knowledge, not just shape, determines whether a value is acceptable.
14. Key Takeaways
blocks.text: 14. Key Takeaways

blocks.content: ["Never trust client input; validate every request at the server boundary, regardless of what client side checks already ran.","Validation, sanitization, and transformation are related but distinct operations, and conflating them causes bugs.","Validation must run after deserialization and before any business logic or side effect.","Schema based validation, whether JSON Schema or DTO annotations, scales far better than hand written per field checks.","Type checks are generic and schema driven; business rule checks are domain specific and often need application state.","Collect all errors for public facing APIs; fail fast is acceptable for simpler internal checks.","Skipping validation is a security failure, not just a correctness one, opening the door to injection style attacks.","Service level validation is the authoritative check; client and gateway validation are optimizations, not substitutes.","A handler that trusts its input completely, with no defensive checks left inside it, is a sign validation upstream is doing its job."]
items: Never trust client input; validate every request at the server boundary, regardless of what client side checks already ran.
Validation, sanitization, and transformation are related but distinct operations, and conflating them causes bugs.
Validation must run after deserialization and before any business logic or side effect.
Schema based validation, whether JSON Schema or DTO annotations, scales far better than hand written per field checks.
Type checks are generic and schema driven; business rule checks are domain specific and often need application state.
Collect all errors for public facing APIs; fail fast is acceptable for simpler internal checks.
Skipping validation is a security failure, not just a correctness one, opening the door to injection style attacks.
Service level validation is the authoritative check; client and gateway validation are optimizations, not substitutes.
A handler that trusts its input completely, with no defensive checks left inside it, is a sign validation upstream is doing its job.

blocks.title: The three stages, together
blocks.content: Routing answers which code runs. Deserialization answers what shape the data takes. Validation and transformation answers whether that data can be trusted. Each stage depends on the one before it, and skipping any of them weakens the ones that follow.

Routing decided which code should run. Deserialization turned raw bytes into a usable object. Validation and transformation made that object something business logic can finally trust. Together, these three stages are what stand between an arbitrary request from the outside world and the safe, predictable input your application code is written to expect.
